issues.legal_issue: The amended coparcenary rights apply only where the daughter and her coparcener parent were both alive when the amendment commenced.
material_facts: The daughter claimed a share in coparcenary property under the amended law.
Her father, from whom the property had devolved, died before the amendment commenced, and the succession shares had crystallized under the law then in force.
issues.conclusion: The amended rights did not apply to the claim because the father was not alive when the amendment commenced. The rights apply to daughters who are alive and whose coparcener parent is also alive at commencement, regardless of when the daughter was born.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1), read with Section 6(3) of the Hindu Succession Act as amended, confers the right on and from commencement and refers to a coparcener's death after commencement. A substantive amendment is prospective unless expressly or by necessary intendment made retrospective; no such indication appears here. The Court applied the plain language of the amendment and the principle in Shyam Sunder v. Ram Kumar, and found no contrary rule in the decisions concerning changes expressly made applicable to pending proceedings, including G. Sekar v. Geetha.

predicates.daughter_claims_amended_coparcenary_righ: A daughter seeks a coparcenary share under an amended succession rule.
predicates.daughter_alive_at_commencement: The daughter was alive when the amendment commenced.
predicates.parent_alive_as_coparcener_at_commenceme: The daughter's parent was alive as a coparcener when the amendment commenced.

issues.definition: When a daughter claims an amended coparcenary right but either she or her coparcener parent was not alive at commencement, the amended right does not apply to her claim.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier dispositions and partitions remain unaffected by the amendment, and a statutory notional partition arising before commencement does not become subject to the amendment's formal-partition rule.
material_facts: The father died before the amendment commenced, causing succession shares to crystallize under the prior law through a notional partition.
The daughter sought to have those shares redefined under the amendment.
The Court considered the effect of the amendment's provisions concerning dispositions and partitions before the statutory cutoff and the definition of partition.
issues.conclusion: Dispositions, alienations and partitions made before the statutory cutoff remain unaffected. A notional partition arising by operation of the prior law is not subject to the amendment's registered-deed-or-court-decree definition. A partition effected after the cutoff is governed by that definition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1)'s proviso and Section 6(5), including its Explanation, preserve the specified earlier transactions and define partition for the amendment's purposes. The provisions must be read harmoniously with the substantive right and cannot be used to reopen transactions valid under the prior law or to treat a statutory notional partition as a formal partition. The Court relied on the interpretive principles discussed in S. Sundaram Pillai v. R. Pattabiraman and Keshavji Ravji & Co. v. CIT, and on the principle that statutory deeming provisions are given full effect as discussed in Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum.

predicates.partition_or_succession_claim: A party seeks a share in property affected by a partition or succession.
predicates.pre_cutoff_transaction: A disposition, alienation or partition was made before the cutoff specified for preserving earlier transactions.
predicates.notional_partition_under_prior_law: A partition was deemed to occur by operation of the prior law when succession opened, rather than being effected by a partition deed or court decree.

issues.definition: In a partition or succession claim, an earlier qualifying transaction or a notional partition under the prior law remains unaffected by the amendment.
